Same bytes. Different lifetime.

Reclaiming unreferenced objects without confusing old work with new data.

A content hash answers “are these bytes the same?” A delayed delete needs a different answer: “is this still the physical object I intended to remove?” Live Snapshot Prune explores that distinction.

The practical idea

Online garbage collection with concurrent uploads, restores, and deletions—and an ABA-style race hiding in the object identity.

Key terms in plain English +

ABA-style race

An identity appears unchanged after the underlying resource has changed. Old work can mistake the new resource for the original one.

Object incarnation

A specific physical lifetime of an object, distinct from the content it happens to hold.

Mark-and-sweep collection

A reclamation approach that identifies reachable objects, then removes candidates judged unreachable.

Lost acknowledgement

An operation may have succeeded remotely, but the caller never receives confirmation.

The problem

A backup system cannot assume that the world stops during garbage collection. Uploads create data, snapshots acquire references, restores read objects, and deletions remove references. A collector can make a valid observation that becomes stale before its external delete actually takes effect.

What the resume describes

The project combines PostgreSQL metadata transactions, independent object storage, snapshot APIs, and online mark-and-sweep collection. Correctness mechanisms distinguish logical content identity from physical object incarnations. A verifier introduces faults across multiple services and validates end-state invariants.

The race, step by step

Imagine an unreferenced object A₁ containing content with hash H. A delete for A₁ is queued but delayed. The same bytes are uploaded again and become live as A₂. If the stale delete addresses only H, it can remove the new live data. The content identity returned to the same value, while the physical lifetime changed: an ABA-style hazard.

The design implication

Deletion needs an identity or precondition that refers to the selected incarnation. The exact storage-key layout and fencing protocol cannot be established from the resume alone. The conceptual lab uses distinct A₁ and A₂ targets to demonstrate why the distinction matters, without presenting it as a reproduction of the implementation.

The tradeoff

Separating identities adds lifecycle metadata and recovery bookkeeping. In return, it gives delayed work a narrower target. A safe design must still explain how retries, lost acknowledgements, and orphan objects are reconciled across the transactional metadata boundary and nontransactional object operations.

Testing the uncertain outcome

The resume reports fault injection for lost acknowledgements, process crashes, restart recovery, concurrent operations, and orphan reclamation. These cases are valuable because a timeout does not reveal whether a remote operation committed. The verifier also checks final invariants rather than treating a successful API response as sufficient evidence.

What remains to verify

A public repository was not found on the supplied profile. The precise invariants, failure schedules, isolation level, object-store guarantees, and verifier logs should accompany a full technical review. The design story here is based on the resume, with conceptual analysis clearly separated from implementation evidence.

Design alternatives, compared

Architectural analysis of the choices described above. These comparisons do not reconstruct undocumented decision history.

Design choices, alternatives, and their tradeoffs
Choice exploredAlternativeWhat changes
Distinguish physical incarnationsDelete by logical content identity aloneNarrows the target of stale work, at the cost of lifecycle metadata and recovery bookkeeping.
Collect while operations continuePause all mutating work for collectionPreserves concurrency, but makes stale observations and interleavings part of the correctness argument.
Test lost acknowledgementsTreat every timeout as a failed operationExplores uncertain remote outcomes and retry safety. End-state invariants must explain what survived.
